title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 207: The Vanishing Melodies: Whistled Speech
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 207 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

The Vanishing Melodies: The Linguistic Science of Whistled Speech

Paragraph 1. Across the world, roughly seventy isolated communities have created an ingenious way to communicate over long distances: whistled speech. Rather than being separate languages, whistled systems transform existing spoken tongues into high-pitched whistles. Well-known examples include Silbo Gomero in Spain's Canary Islands, whistled Turkish in mountain villages, and whistled Yupik in the Arctic. While human shouting reaches only eighty decibels and becomes unclear beyond two hundred metres, a clear whistle hits one hundred and thirty decibels and carries across deep canyons for up to ten kilometres.

Paragraph 2. Producing whistled speech relies on a surprisingly simple physical method. During normal speaking, our vocal cords vibrate inside the throat to form words. In whistled speech, however, the vocal cords stay completely still; sound is created solely by pushing compressed air through a narrow gap between the tongue, teeth, and lips. Whistlers copy the rising and falling pitch of spoken vowels and replace consonants with sharp pitch jumps or sudden pauses. Remarkably, skilled listeners understand more than ninety percent of whistled messages.

Paragraph 3. Whistled speech has also challenged old beliefs about how the human brain processes language. Textbooks long taught that spoken words are handled mainly by the left half of the brain, while the right half interprets music, melody, and emotional tone. When neuroscientist Dr. Onur Güntürkün scanned Turkish villagers fluent in both spoken and whistled Turkish, spoken words lit up only the left side as expected. Yet when subjects listened to whistled sentences, scans showed strong, equal activity across both brain halves at once, blending musical and language centres together.

Paragraph 4. Historically, whistled speech grew in steep mountains, dense forests, and vast wetlands where travelling on foot was slow and exhausting. Shepherds on La Gomera could chat across wide valleys without climbing down steep paths. Today, modern life threatens these traditions. Mobile phones, cars, and paved roads have replaced long-distance whistling, while young villagers moving to cities often hide the skill because urban society treats it as backward.

Paragraph 5. To stop whistled languages from dying out, several communities have launched rescue plans. In 1999, La Gomera's government made Silbo Gomero a compulsory subject in all primary and secondary schools, reaching over twenty thousand students every year. Elsewhere, linguists use artificial intelligence software to save the sound patterns of elderly whistlers in the Caucasus mountains before the last fluent elders pass away.

q6.text: Loud shouting can be understood clearly from a distance of ten kilometres.

steps: Đoạn 1: Tiếng hét chỉ nghe rõ trong khoảng 200 mét, chỉ tiếng huýt sáo mới đi xa được 10 km.

q7.text: During whistled speech, a speaker's vocal cords remain completely still.

steps: Đoạn 3: Tiếng huýt sáo kích hoạt đồng đều cả 2 bán cầu não (both brain halves at once).

q9.text: Whistled languages originally grew in flat desert areas with easy transport.

steps: Đoạn 4: Phát triển ở vùng núi dốc, rừng rậm, đầm lầy nơi đi bộ rất khó khăn.

steps: Đoạn 5: Chỉ nói đây là môn bắt buộc ở trường phổ thông, không nhắc điều kiện thi đại học.
